title: Vita Sancti Hilarionis
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0162.stoa063.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Eorum enim qui fecere, virtus (ut ait Crispus) tanta habetur, quantum 3 eam verbis potuere extollere praeclara ingenia. Alexander Magnus Macedo, quem vel arietem 4, vel pardum, vel hi cum caprarum Daniel vocat, cum ad Achillis tumulum pervenisset : Felicem te 5, ait, juvenis, qui magno frueris [Al. fruaris] praecone meritorum I Home- rum videlicet significans. Porro mihi tanti ac talis viri conversatio [Al. conversio], Vitaque dicenda (??)st, ut Homerus quoque si adesset, vel invideret materiae, vel succumberet. Quanquam enim san- ctus Fpiphanius Salaminae Cypri episcopus, qui cum Hilarione plurimum versatus est, laudem ejus brevi epistola scripserit 6, quae vulgo legitur;
passages.english: For the virtue of those who have done [great deeds] is reckoned, as Crispus says, to be as great as brilliant minds have been able to exalt it in words. Alexander the Great of Macedon, whom Daniel calls either a ram, or a leopard, or a he-goat, when he had come to the tomb of Achilles, said: "Happy are you, young man, who enjoy a great herald of your merits," meaning, of course, Homer. But I have to tell of the way of life and the Life of so great and so remarkable a man that Homer too, if he were present, would either envy the subject matter or sink beneath it. For although the holy Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, who spent a great deal of time with Hilarion, wrote his praise in a short letter which is commonly read,
passages.notes: Crispus is Sallust (Gaius Sallustius Crispus); the sentence paraphrases Catiline 8. The scanned text reads "vel hi cum caprarum", which is evidently corrupt; it probably stands for "vel hircum caprarum" ("he-goat of the goats", cf. Daniel 8), and I have translated it on that basis. Some witnesses read "fruaris" ("may you enjoy") for "frueris". "Conversatio" (way of life) has a variant "conversio" (conversion). Footnote numerals and scanning errors have been corrected silently: "dicenda (??)st" read as "dicenda est", "Fpiphanius" as "Epiphanius".
